doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Section 3 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 defines the statutory offence of money-laundering. Under this provision, whosoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge, or knowingly assists, or knowingly is a party, or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime—including its concealment, possession, acquisition, or use—and projecting or claiming it as untainted property commits the offence of money-laundering. For banking compliance investigators, Section 3 establishes why multi-hop transfer networks that obscure the origin of funds trigger reporting obligations. Compliance analysts and automated decision-support systems do not adjudicate criminal guilt under Section 3; rather, they document objective transaction indicators that create reasonable grounds to suspect involvement with proceeds of crime for Principal Officer review.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: The Explanation inserted into Section 3 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 clarifies two vital evidentiary principles for financial intelligence reviews. First, a person falls within the statutory scope if directly or indirectly involved in any process or activity connected with proceeds of crime across concealment, possession, acquisition, use, projecting as untainted property, or claiming as untainted property in any manner whatsoever, even when each act stands independently. Second, the process or activity connected with proceeds of crime is a continuing activity and continues until such time a person is directly or indirectly enjoying the proceeds of crime by concealment, possession, acquisition, use, or projection. Staggered transfers executed weeks after initial receipt therefore remain relevant to an active review.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Read alongside Section 2(1)(u) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002, proceeds of crime encompass any property derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, by any person as a result of criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence, or the value of any such property. When funds are dispersed from a seed account into multiple intermediary accounts and later consolidated into a common beneficiary account, the layering sequence obscures the audit trail linking source and destination. Under Section 3, knowingly assisting such concealment or pass-through movement through mule accounts implicates the layering stage of money-laundering. Investigators evaluating scatter-gather topologies should assess whether intermediary hops lack commercial substance, verified invoices, or genuine economic justification before recommending escalation to the Principal Officer.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Section 3 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 expressly extends beyond completed laundering schemes to cover direct or indirect attempts and knowing assistance. In banking operations, an entity or individual who permits an account to be operated as a conduit or mule pass-through account—receiving dispersed credits and forwarding near-identical balances onward while retaining a percentage commission—may provide knowing assistance in concealing proceeds. Because bank compliance units lack judicial authority to verify underlying predicate offences, investigators must record observable financial anomalies such as fee skimming, rapid velocity, and uncorroborated commercial claims while explicitly noting missing external evidence and refraining from making definitive criminal guilt assertions in investigation worksheets.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Section 12(1)(a) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 mandates that every reporting entity—including banking companies, financial institutions, and financial intermediaries—shall maintain a record of all transactions, including information relating to transactions covered under clause (b), in such manner as to enable it to reconstruct individual transactions. Transaction reconstructability is the statutory cornerstone of AML fund-flow tracing. When reconstructing scatter-gather paths across RTGS, NEFT, IMPS, and internal transfers, banks must preserve exact timestamps, sender and receiver account identifiers, exact INR decimal amounts, and payment references so an independent auditor or FIU-IND examiner can trace every leg without ambiguity or rounding distortion.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Under Section 12(1)(b) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002, every reporting entity is legally obligated to furnish to the Director of the Financial Intelligence Unit - India (FIU-IND), within such time as may be prescribed under the Maintenance of Records Rules, information relating to prescribed transactions, whether attempted or executed, the nature and value of which may be prescribed. This statutory duty encompasses Cash Transaction Reports, Cross-Border Wire Transfer Reports, Counterfeit Currency Reports, Non-Profit Organisation Transaction Reports, and Suspicious Transaction Reports. Attempted suspicious transactions that are aborted or partially blocked before settlement still require full documentation and assessment for statutory reporting under Section 12(1)(b).

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Clauses (c), (d), and (e) of Section 12(1) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 require every reporting entity to maintain records of documents evidencing the identity of its clients and beneficial owners, as well as account files and business correspondence relating to its clients. In complex investigations involving multi-entity scatter-gather flows, preserving verified KYC records, beneficial ownership declarations, commercial registry checks, and historical counterparty correspondence allows analysts to test benign explanations against suspicious layering hypotheses. Incomplete account files, missing KYC records, or unverified corporate signatories constitute material evidentiary gaps that must be surfaced in the investigation worksheet rather than overlooked during disposition review.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Section 12(2) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 mandates that every information maintained, furnished, or verified—save as otherwise provided under any law for the time being in force—shall be kept confidential. Reporting entities, compliance analysts, and technology systems supporting AML alert triage must safeguard investigation worksheets, STR drafts, escalation rationales, and FIU-IND correspondence against unauthorized disclosure. In particular, customers under active alert investigation must never be alerted or tipped off that their transactions are undergoing suspicious activity scrutiny or that a Suspicious Transaction Report is being prepared for submission to the Director, FIU-IND, as disclosure compromises statutory intelligence gathering.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Sub-sections (3) and (4) of Section 12 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 prescribe mandatory five-year retention periods for AML compliance records. Transaction records maintained under Section 12(1)(a) must be preserved for a period of five years from the date of the transaction between a client and the reporting entity. Identity documents, beneficial ownership records, account files, and business correspondence maintained under Section 12(1)(e) must be preserved for five years after the business relationship between a client and the reporting entity has ended or the account has been closed, whichever is later. Retention ensures historical counterparty patterns remain verifiable during multi-year inquiries.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Section 12A(1) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 empowers the Director of the Financial Intelligence Unit - India (FIU-IND) to call for from any reporting entity any of the records referred to in Section 11A, Section 12(1), or Section 12AA(1), as well as any additional information considered necessary for the purposes of the Act. This statutory access authority means that every alert disposition—whether escalated as an STR, placed on request for additional information, or closed as benign—must retain complete supporting transaction logs, deterministic calculation traces, KYC records, and registry checks in an immutable audit trail capable of prompt production upon regulatory demand from FIU-IND.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 12A of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 obligate every reporting entity to furnish to the Director, FIU-IND any information called for under Section 12A(1) within such time and in such manner as specified, while mandating that information sought under this section shall be kept strictly confidential. Banks cannot invoke general banker-customer secrecy to refuse statutory information calls from FIU-IND. Conversely, reporting entities must protect the confidentiality of FIU-IND information requests internally and never notify the affected customer that records or supplementary transaction logs were called for under Section 12A. Reconstructable five-year record retention encompasses transaction ledgers, exact decimal amounts, KYC identity documents, beneficial ownership filings, business correspondence, and written investigation analysis so the reporting entity can respond swiftly and accurately to supervisory audits or Section 12A requests from FIU-IND.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Section 12AA(1) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 requires every reporting entity, prior to the commencement of each specified transaction, to perform Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD). Under clauses (a) and (b), the reporting entity must verify the identity of clients undertaking specified transactions using prescribed authentication methods and take additional steps to examine the ownership and financial position, including sources of funds, of the client. When an account exhibits high-value scatter-gather volume sharply exceeding its declared annual income or business scale, Section 12AA mandates substantive verification of ownership structure and source of funds before treating the activity as economically legitimate.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Under Section 12AA(1)(c) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002, a reporting entity must take additional steps as prescribed to record the purpose behind conducting a specified transaction and the intended nature of the relationship between the transaction parties. Under Section 12AA(2), where the client fails to fulfill the Enhanced Due Diligence conditions laid down in sub-section (1), the reporting entity shall not allow the specified transaction to be carried out. In alert triage, when commercial purpose or counterparty relationships cannot be corroborated from existing KYC and registry records, analysts must not close the case as benign and must instead escalate or formally request corroborating documentation.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Section 12AA(3) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 mandates that where any specified transaction or series of specified transactions undertaken by a client is considered suspicious or likely to involve proceeds of crime, the reporting entity shall increase the future monitoring of the business relationship with the client, including greater scrutiny of transactions in such manner as may be prescribed. Section 12AA(4) further requires that information obtained while applying Enhanced Due Diligence measures under Section 12AA shall be maintained for a period of five years from the date of the transaction, ensuring full traceability for subsequent FIU-IND reviews and supervisory inspections.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 2(1)(g) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 defines a 'suspicious transaction' as a transaction referred to in clause (h), including an attempted transaction, whether or not made in cash, which to a person acting in good faith gives rise to a reasonable ground of suspicion that it may involve proceeds of an offence specified in the Schedule to the Act, regardless of the value involved, or appears to be made in circumstances of unusual or unjustified complexity. Crucially, the definition carries zero minimum monetary threshold: even modest-value multi-hop layering or attempted pass-through transfers qualify for STR evaluation when complexity lacks legitimate economic basis.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Under sub-clauses (iii) and (iv) of Rule 2(1)(g) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, a transaction also constitutes a suspicious transaction if, to a person acting in good faith, it appears to have no economic rationale or bona fide purpose, or gives rise to a reasonable ground of suspicion that it may involve financing of activities relating to terrorism. In scatter-gather alert reviews, demonstrating the absence of economic rationale requires examining both suspicious topology (dispersion, intermediary skimming, rapid or staggered reconsolidation) and benign commercial hypotheses (registered marketplace escrow, corporate payroll, licensed chit pools, or verifiable charity relief) before concluding whether reasonable grounds of suspicion exist.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 2(1)(h) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 broadly defines a 'transaction' to include a purchase, sale, loan, pledge, gift, transfer, delivery, or the arrangement thereof, encompassing deposits, withdrawals, exchanges, credits, debits, electronic fund transfers, and opening of accounts. Rule 2(1)(fa) defines 'Non-Profit Organisation' for AML monitoring as any entity or organisation constituted for religious or charitable purposes referred to in Section 2(15) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and registered as a trust, society, or Section 8 company. Understanding both definitions ensures electronic IMPS, NEFT, RTGS, and charitable trust pools fall squarely within reconstructable record obligations.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 3(1)(A) and Rule 3(1)(B) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 require every reporting entity to maintain records of all cash transactions of the value of more than rupees ten lakhs (INR 10,00,000) or its equivalent in foreign currency, as well as all series of cash transactions integrally connected to each other which have been individually valued below rupees ten lakhs or its equivalent in foreign currency where such series of transactions have taken place within a month and the monthly aggregate exceeds ten lakh rupees. Splitting deposits or transfers into multiple tranches just below INR 10,00,000 within a rolling monthly window is classic structuring requiring aggregation and review.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 3(1)(BA) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 requires reporting entities to maintain dedicated records of all transactions involving receipts by non-profit organisations of value more than rupees ten lakhs (INR 10,00,000), or its equivalent in foreign currency. When an alert involves a charitable trust, society, or NGO receiving pooled donations exceeding ten lakh rupees and disbursing funds to multiple regional accounts, investigators must verify active DARPAN portal registration, Section 80G status, and alignment with charitable relief activities while ensuring NPO Transaction Report (NTR) record obligations under Rule 3(1)(BA) are respected. Non-Profit Organisation and charitable trust alerts require verifying NITI Aayog DARPAN portal registration, Section 80G or 12A status, trustee beneficial ownership, and transparent alignment between donor inflows and verified charitable relief disbursements, while ensuring Rule 3(1)(BA) reporting thresholds above INR 10,00,000 are monitored.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 3(1)(C) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 covers all cash transactions where forged or counterfeit currency notes or bank notes have been used as genuine or where any forgery of a valuable security or document has taken place. Rule 3(1)(D) mandates record maintenance for all suspicious transactions—whether or not made in cash—and by way of deposits, credits, withdrawals, electronic transfers, remittances, or settlements, regardless of the transaction value. Consequently, non-cash electronic layering via NEFT, RTGS, or IMPS triggers Rule 3(1)(D) preservation and STR assessment even when zero physical cash enters the transaction network. Suspicious transaction obligations cover executed and attempted transactions, cash and non-cash electronic rails alike, with zero minimum monetary threshold whenever objective anomalies create reasonable grounds of suspicion or demonstrate unusual complexity lacking apparent economic rationale or bona fide lawful purpose.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 3(1)(E) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 mandates that reporting entities maintain records of all cross-border wire transfers of the value of more than five lakh rupees (INR 5,00,000) or its equivalent in foreign currency where either the origin or destination of the fund is in India. Rule 3(1)(F) extends mandatory record keeping to all purchase and sale by any person of immovable property valued at fifty lakh rupees (INR 50,00,000) or more that is registered by the reporting entity. Cross-border wire legs exceeding INR 5,00,000 must preserve complete originator and beneficiary identification to support both CBWTR filing and cross-bank fund-flow reconstruction.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 4 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 specifies the mandatory particulars that every transaction record maintained under Rule 3 must contain: (a) the nature of the transactions, (b) the amount of the transaction and the currency in which it was denominated, (c) the date on which the transaction was conducted, and (d) the parties to the transaction. When reconstructing candidate fund-flow paths during an AML investigation, preserving exact Rule 4 fields—including exact INR Decimal amounts, payment channel, timestamps, and counterparty account identifiers—ensures every finding can be deterministically audited against core banking records without approximation. Reconstructable five-year record retention encompasses transaction ledgers, exact decimal amounts, KYC identity documents, beneficial ownership filings, business correspondence, and written investigation analysis so the reporting entity can respond swiftly and accurately to supervisory audits or Section 12A requests from FIU-IND.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 5 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 directs that every reporting entity shall maintain information in respect of transactions with its client referred to in Rule 3 in accordance with the procedure and manner specified by its regulator, such as the Reserve Bank of India, from time to time. It further requires reporting entities to evolve an internal mechanism for maintaining such information in such form and at such intervals as specified, enabling rapid retrieval for internal audits, Principal Officer escalations, and regulatory calls by FIU-IND. Structured evidence registries with immutable IDs directly operationalize Rule 5 traceability.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 7(1) and Rule 7(2) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 require every reporting entity to communicate to the Director, FIU-IND the name, designation, and address of its Principal Officer and Designated Director. The Principal Officer is statutorily designated to furnish the information referred to in Rule 3 to the Director, FIU-IND on the basis of information available with the reporting entity. Automated alert engines and AI investigation agents cannot independently submit STRs to FIU-IND; they function strictly as decision-support systems preparing evidence-grounded worksheets for review and formal sign-off by the compliance analyst and Principal Officer.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 7(3) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 mandates that every reporting entity shall evolve an internal mechanism having regard to any guidelines issued by the Director, FIU-IND in consultation with its sectoral regulator, for detecting transactions referred to in Rule 3 and for furnishing information about such transactions in such form as may be directed. Rule 7(4) imposes a duty on every reporting entity, its Designated Director, officers, and employees to observe the procedure and manner of furnishing information specified by the Director. Documented alert triage protocols, dual-hypothesis analysis, and human approval gates fulfill Rule 7(3) governance expectations.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 8(1) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 sets the statutory reporting schedule for periodic threshold-based disclosures to FIU-IND. The Principal Officer of a reporting entity shall furnish the information in respect of transactions referred to in clauses (A), (B), (BA), (C), and (E) of sub-rule (1) of Rule 3—covering Cash Transaction Reports above INR 10 lakhs, integrally connected cash series, NPO receipts above INR 10 lakhs, counterfeit currency transactions, and Cross-Border Wire Transfers above INR 5 lakhs—every month to the Director, FIU-IND by the 15th day of the succeeding month. Timely triage protects statutory compliance with PMLR Rule 8 deadlines: periodic CTR, NTR, and CBWTR filings by the 15th day of the succeeding month, and Suspicious Transaction Reports furnished promptly and not later than seven working days after the Principal Officer is satisfied that reasonable grounds of suspicion exist.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 8(2) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 governs the statutory deadline for filing Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs). The Principal Officer of a reporting entity shall furnish the information referred to in clause (D) of sub-rule (1) of Rule 3 promptly in writing, or by fax or electronic mail, to the Director, FIU-IND not later than seven working days on being satisfied that the transaction is suspicious. The seven working-day clock begins upon the Principal Officer's satisfaction of reasonable grounds of suspicion following investigation, making timely alert triage, bounded replanning, and clear evidentiary packaging essential for statutory compliance.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Sub-rules (3) through (5) of Rule 8 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 specify that immovable property transaction records under Rule 3(1)(F) must be furnished quarterly by the 15th day of the month succeeding the quarter, and reinforce that delayed internal investigation workflows cannot justify missing the seven working-day STR deadline once suspicion is established. Where an analyst lacks external inter-bank logs needed to resolve ambiguity, issuing a structured request for information prevents premature closure while preserving audit documentation of when sufficient evidence was assembled for the Principal Officer's satisfaction under Rule 8(2). Timely triage protects statutory compliance with PMLR Rule 8 deadlines: periodic CTR, NTR, and CBWTR filings by the 15th day of the succeeding month, and Suspicious Transaction Reports furnished promptly and not later than seven working days after the Principal Officer is satisfied that reasonable grounds of suspicion exist.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 9(1) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 requires every reporting entity, at the commencement of an account-based relationship, to identify its clients, verify their identity, obtain information on the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship, and determine whether a client is acting on behalf of a beneficial owner. Reporting entities must also conduct Client Due Diligence for occasional transactions equal to or exceeding INR 50,000, international money transfers, or whenever there is a suspicion of money-laundering or doubts about the veracity or adequacy of previously obtained customer identification data. Applying Enhanced Due Diligence requires verifying source of funds, source of wealth, beneficial ownership, and economic rationale whenever observed turnover diverges materially from declared annual income or occupation. Analysts record every verified KYC identifier, highlight unresolved income-to-volume discrepancies, and document enhanced ongoing monitoring recommendations.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 9(3) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, as amended in March 2023, establishes the statutory thresholds for identifying the natural person Beneficial Owner (BO) behind legal entities. Where the client is a company, the beneficial owner is the natural person(s) who, acting alone or together or through one or more juridical persons, has a controlling ownership interest of more than 10 percent of the shares, capital, or profits of the company, or exercises control through other means. For partnership firms, the threshold is ownership of or entitlement to more than 10 percent of capital or profits (revised down from 15 percent in 2023). Identifying opaque corporate BOs is critical when assessing suspected shell entities.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
clause_number: Rule 9(3)(c)-(f) (Beneficial Owner — Trusts & Senior Managing Official)
text: Under Rule 9(3)(e) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 (as amended in 2023), where the client is a trust, identification of beneficial owners shall include identification of the author of the trust, the trustee, the beneficiaries with 10 percent or more interest in the trust, and any other natural person exercising ultimate effective control over the trust through a chain of control or ownership. Where no natural person is identified through ownership thresholds, Rule 9(3)(d) directs reporting entities to identify the relevant natural person who holds the position of senior managing official. Trust and NGO accounts handling pooled relief disbursements require complete trustee and beneficiary verification.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 9(9A) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, introduced by the 2023 amendment, requires every banking company or financial institution to register the details of a client, in case of a client being a Non-Profit Organisation (NPO), on the DARPAN Portal of NITI Aayog, if not already registered, and maintain such registration records for a period of five years after the business relationship has ended or the account has been closed. During AML investigations of charitable trusts or NGOs exhibiting scatter-gather disbursements, verifying DARPAN and Section 80G credentials is a mandatory documentary step before assessing whether charitable payouts are benign.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 9(12) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 mandates that every reporting entity shall exercise ongoing due diligence with respect to the business relationship with every client and closely examine the transactions in order to ensure that they are consistent with their knowledge of the client, his business and risk profile, and where necessary, the source of funds. Ongoing due diligence requires comparing observed account credits and debits against declared annual income, occupation, commercial registration status, and historical counterparty cadence. Sharp deviations—such as a low-income individual routing multi-lakh business-like pass-through flows—trigger escalated review under Rule 9(12).

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Sub-rules (14) and (15) of Rule 9 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 require reporting entities to adopt regulator-prescribed KYC policies, upload KYC records to the Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR), and apply risk-based verification proportionate to client risk categorization. Enhanced monitoring applies whenever a client's risk category is high, corporate ownership is layered, or transactions diverge from expected profile. Maintaining synchronized CKYCR and internal KYC records enables investigators to verify whether an account's KYC tier is current or requires immediate remediation via fresh Customer Due Diligence. Risk categorization guides monitoring intensity and periodic KYC refresh intervals (two years for High risk, eight years for Medium risk, ten years for Low risk) without serving as a standalone verdict. Investigators weigh risk tier alongside reconstructed fund-flow paths, commercial corroboration, and counterparty cadence when recommending disposition.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: In operational AML typologies mapped to Section 3 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002, concealment of proceeds of crime commonly unfolds through placement, layering, and integration. Scatter-gather networks exemplify the layering stage: a root account fragments a principal sum across several unrelated mule or intermediary accounts, sometimes across multiple tiers of four to five hops or staggered across fourteen to thirty days, before reconsolidating funds into a single beneficiary. Separating the financial origin from the ultimate recipient is a hallmark of concealment under Section 3, provided investigators first rule out legitimate commercial pooling or settlement mechanisms. Operational verification requires reconstructing candidate multi-hop paths across bounded lookback windows, checking exact decimal conservation between dispersed outflows and consolidated inflows, and testing whether intermediary accounts hold verified commercial registrations or recurring prior counterparty history before escalating an alert for Suspicious Transaction Report review.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Although criminal prosecution under Section 3 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 ultimately depends on proceeds connected to a scheduled offence listed in the Schedule to the Act, reporting entities and bank compliance investigators are neither equipped nor expected to prove a predicate crime before escalating a Suspicious Transaction Report. Instead, bank investigations examine financial indicators—such as unexplained pass-through velocity, structured tranches below reporting thresholds, unverified shell counterparties, and commission skimming—and refer reasonable grounds of suspicion to FIU-IND so statutory enforcement agencies can investigate potential predicate links. Reasonable-grounds reporting balances preventing false-negative misses of genuine layering against avoiding defensive over-reporting of verified commercial look-alikes. Analysts present neutral, evidence-backed findings without ever asserting criminal guilt or declaring that a predicate offence has been judicially proven.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: To satisfy the transaction reconstruction mandate of Section 12(1)(a) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002, banks must maintain linked records across all domestic and international payment rails, including RTGS, NEFT, IMPS, UPI, cheque clearing, and SWIFT wire transfers. When a transaction chain exits the reporting bank to an external correspondent bank and later re-enters or terminates off-book, internal transaction records cannot reconstruct the missing external leg. Under Section 12 reconstructability principles, investigators must flag external-bank visibility gaps explicitly as missing evidence and request inter-bank logs rather than extrapolating unobserved transfers. Wire transfer compliance across RTGS, NEFT, IMPS, and cross-border channels mandates retaining accurate originator and beneficiary account identifiers, unique transaction references, and batch reconciliation records so end-to-end fund flows remain fully traceable and any cross-border transfers exceeding INR 5,00,000 satisfy statutory reporting.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Section 12(1)(e) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 requires banks to retain verified identity records, business correspondence, and account files for all clients and beneficial owners. When evaluating whether a high-value scatter-gather flow represents legitimate commercial settlement—such as e-commerce seller payouts, wholesale trade settlements, or corporate payroll runs—investigators rely on retained corporate registration records (MCA CIN, GSTIN filings, PAN, board resolutions) and historical account correspondence. Absence of verifiable commercial registration records undermines a benign commercial hypothesis and prevents automatic closure of the alert. Corroborating a benign commercial hypothesis requires independent confirmation of active statutory registration (GSTIN, MCA CIN, or relevant sector licence) paired with recurring multi-month counterparty settlement history and alignment between observed payment ticket sizes and declared business turnover; a single registry flag alone is insufficient.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Because Section 12A of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 authorizes the Director, FIU-IND to demand underlying transaction logs, KYC files, EDD records, and supplementary analysis from any reporting entity, every disposition worksheet must be self-contained and audit-defensible. Each material assertion in an investigation report should cite immutable internal evidence identifiers (transaction IDs, KYC record IDs, commercial registry checks, reconstructed path IDs, and deterministic calculation IDs) together with the specific statutory provisions applied, ensuring seamless response to any subsequent Section 12A inquiry. End-to-end compliance governance combines deterministic safety verification, dual-hypothesis reporting, explicit missing-evidence disclosure, and cryptographic SHA-256 human analyst approval so every committed disposition remains transparent, auditable, and strictly under human control. Automated systems never file regulatory reports autonomously and always preserve immutable evidence references for Principal Officer and supervisory audit review.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Enhanced Due Diligence under Section 12AA of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 is triggered whenever transaction patterns exhibit unusual complexity or value disproportionate to the client's verified financial position. For example, if a savings account holder with modest declared annual income suddenly orchestrates multi-lakh outbound transfers across unrelated counterparties without corresponding business registration or documented source of funds, Section 12AA requires examining the underlying financial position and source of wealth. Failing to corroborate source of funds bars benign clearance and supports escalation or formal information request. Applying Enhanced Due Diligence requires verifying source of funds, source of wealth, beneficial ownership, and economic rationale whenever observed turnover diverges materially from declared annual income or occupation. Analysts record every verified KYC identifier, highlight unresolved income-to-volume discrepancies, and document enhanced ongoing monitoring recommendations.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002
text: Under Section 12AA(3) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002, when a client's specified transactions are assessed as suspicious or likely to involve proceeds of crime, reporting entities must intensify ongoing monitoring of the entire business relationship. Heightened monitoring includes lowering alert thresholds for future velocity spikes, reviewing new counterparties and beneficial owners, and periodically re-evaluating the client's risk categorization. Documenting recommended enhanced monitoring steps alongside an STR escalation or request-for-information disposition strengthens institutional compliance with Section 12AA(3). Applying Enhanced Due Diligence requires verifying source of funds, source of wealth, beneficial ownership, and economic rationale whenever observed turnover diverges materially from declared annual income or occupation. Analysts record every verified KYC identifier, highlight unresolved income-to-volume discrepancies, and document enhanced ongoing monitoring recommendations.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 2(1)(g) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 anchors suspicious transaction determination in the objective standard of 'a person acting in good faith' forming a 'reasonable ground of suspicion.' Good-faith assessment requires weighing both inculpatory anomalies and exculpatory commercial evidence impartially without confirmation bias. Moreover, Rule 2(1)(g) explicitly captures attempted transactions: even if a customer aborts a suspicious layered transfer after being asked for supporting invoices or source-of-funds documentation, the attempted transaction remains reportable as an STR to FIU-IND. Reasonable-grounds reporting balances preventing false-negative misses of genuine layering against avoiding defensive over-reporting of verified commercial look-alikes. Analysts present neutral, evidence-backed findings without ever asserting criminal guilt or declaring that a predicate offence has been judicially proven.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Under Rule 3(1)(B) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, reporting entities must aggregate cash transactions that are integrally connected and individually placed below INR 10,00,000 whenever their monthly aggregate crosses the ten-lakh threshold. Common structuring indicators include multiple cash deposits of INR 9,00,000 to INR 9,90,000 across consecutive days, coordinated deposits into multiple related accounts, or split cash withdrawals immediately converted into electronic transfers. Deliberate evasion of the Rule 3(1)(A) CTR threshold also independently triggers Rule 3(1)(D) STR scrutiny. Investigators examining suspected threshold evasion must aggregate linked cash or electronic legs across rolling monthly windows using exact decimal sums, inspect timing proximity across related accounts, and distinguish deliberate sub-INR 10,00,000 fragmentation from legitimate recurring commercial billing schedules backed by verifiable GST invoices.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 3(1)(D) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 makes clear that suspicious transaction record-keeping and reporting apply equally whether or not the transactions are conducted in cash. Digital payment networks—such as rapid IMPS fan-out from a seed account into multiple personal savings accounts followed by RTGS or NEFT consolidation into a single beneficiary—fall squarely within Rule 3(1)(D). Because electronic pass-through schemes avoid cash-counter detection, graph-based path reconstruction and decimal conservation checks are vital for identifying suspicious non-cash layering. Operational verification requires reconstructing candidate multi-hop paths across bounded lookback windows, checking exact decimal conservation between dispersed outflows and consolidated inflows, and testing whether intermediary accounts hold verified commercial registrations or recurring prior counterparty history before escalating an alert for Suspicious Transaction Report review.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 3(1)(E) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 requires reporting entities to record and report all cross-border wire transfers exceeding INR 5,00,000 (or foreign currency equivalent) where either origin or destination lies in India. When domestic scatter-gather consolidation feeds directly into an outward cross-border wire or originates from an inward foreign remittance above INR 5,00,000, analysts must verify complete originator, intermediary, and beneficiary details, check for trade invoice corroboration, and flag any missing correspondent leg information as an evidentiary deficiency. Wire transfer compliance across RTGS, NEFT, IMPS, and cross-border channels mandates retaining accurate originator and beneficiary account identifiers, unique transaction references, and batch reconciliation records so end-to-end fund flows remain fully traceable and any cross-border transfers exceeding INR 5,00,000 satisfy statutory reporting.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 3(1)(BA) and Rule 3(1)(F) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 target two sectors vulnerable to value layering: Non-Profit Organisation receipts above INR 10,00,000 and registered immovable property transactions of INR 50,00,000 or more. In AML alert investigations, rapid pass-through of pooled donations through an unregistered charitable trust or sudden multi-party consolidation purportedly for real-estate purchase without matching sale deeds or registered counterparties warrants Enhanced Due Diligence rather than routine benign closure. Non-Profit Organisation and charitable trust alerts require verifying NITI Aayog DARPAN portal registration, Section 80G or 12A status, trustee beneficial ownership, and transparent alignment between donor inflows and verified charitable relief disbursements, while ensuring Rule 3(1)(BA) reporting thresholds above INR 10,00,000 are monitored.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 4 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 mandates accurate recording of transaction amount, currency, date, nature, and transacting parties. Because regulatory reports and Principal Officer STR filings rely on exact INR figures, calculating cumulative outflows, consolidated inflows, fee retention differences, and retention percentages must be performed with exact decimal precision rather than floating-point approximations or mental estimates. Any discrepancy exceeding one paisa (INR 0.01) between narrative summaries and deterministic transaction totals undermines Rule 4 record fidelity. Every monetary total, outflow-to-inflow variance, fee retention percentage, and structuring threshold comparison must originate from deterministic Python Decimal computation rather than LLM estimation, maintaining exact INR 0.01 grounding across structured schedules and narrative text. Whenever a prose figure deviates by more than one paisa from calc logs or ledger outputs, deterministic verification blocks submission for repair.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 5 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 requires reporting entities to maintain internal mechanisms that preserve transaction information in prescribed regulator-approved formats. doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
clause_number: Rule 7 (Role of Principal Officer in Escalation Review)
text: Under Rule 7 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, the Principal Officer serves as the statutory decision-maker accountable for reviewing escalated alerts and submitting verified STRs to FIU-IND. Statutory reporting authority rests exclusively with the designated Principal Officer notified to FIU-IND. Investigation worksheets prepared by analysts or AI decision-support agents must package both competing hypotheses, exact evidence IDs, and verified citations to enable timely Principal Officer review and formal approval.

text: Rule 7(3) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 directs every reporting entity to calibrate its internal transaction-monitoring and alert-detection mechanisms in accordance with guidelines issued by FIU-IND and sectoral regulators such as the Reserve Bank of India. doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Under Rule 8(2) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, the seven working-day STR submission deadline is triggered once the Principal Officer is satisfied that a transaction is suspicious. doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 9 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 specifies distinct identity verification documents for legal entities—companies, partnership firms, trusts, and proprietorships—including Certificate of Incorporation, Memorandum and Articles of Association, PAN, GST registration, and board resolutions identifying authorized signatories. When an alert involves a purported commercial aggregator, payroll employer, or wholesale trader executing scatter-gather payments, confirming active statutory registration and corroborating recurring counterparty settlement history under Rule 9 is essential before concluding benign commercial activity. Corroborating a benign commercial hypothesis requires independent confirmation of active statutory registration (GSTIN, MCA CIN, or relevant sector licence) paired with recurring multi-month counterparty settlement history and alignment between observed payment ticket sizes and declared business turnover; a single registry flag alone is insufficient.

doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
clause_number: Rule 9 (Enhanced Checks for High-Risk & Shell Counterparties)
text: Under Rule 9 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, reporting entities must verify not only formal registration documents but also the substantive nature of the client's business and beneficial ownership. A newly incorporated or unregistered entity claiming wholesale trade or agency brokerage without active GST filings, valid MCA CIN, or historical supplier-buyer relationships displays classic shell-entity characteristics. Because forged or dormant registrations can be misused to mask mule networks, registration status must be corroborated against counterparty history length and transaction cadence. Distinguishing genuine commercial traders from shell conduits requires corroborating corporate registration records (MCA CIN, active GSTIN filings, proprietorship licences) alongside multi-month counterparty history and beneficial ownership disclosures. Contradictions between claimed trade narrations and authoritative registry lookups prohibit automatic benign closure.

text: Rule 9 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, read with RBI KYC Master Directions, requires reporting entities to maintain risk management systems to determine whether a client or beneficial owner is a Politically Exposed Person (PEP). Where a PEP or close relative/associate is involved in high-value multi-hop transfers, reporting entities must obtain senior management approval for continuing the relationship, take reasonable measures to establish source of wealth and source of funds, and subject the account to heightened ongoing transaction monitoring. doc_title: Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
text: Rule 9 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 mandates ongoing due diligence and periodic KYC updation to keep client identification and risk profiles accurate over time. clause_number: Rule 7 & Rule 8 (No Tipping Off During Information Requests)
text: When an investigation recommends requesting additional information—such as invoices, GST filings, commercial contracts, or source-of-funds explanations—compliance teams operating under Rules 7 and 8 of the PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 and Section 12(2) of PMLA 2002 must frame customer outreach strictly as routine KYC or transaction-monitoring verification. Staff must never reveal that an AML alert was triggered, that scatter-gather layering is suspected, or that an STR is under consideration for FIU-IND submission, preserving strict anti-tipping-off confidentiality throughout the inquiry. Strict anti-tipping-off controls bar disclosing STR consideration, internal alert triggers, or FIU-IND correspondence to customers or unauthorized third parties. Any necessary customer document requests must be framed neutrally as standard KYC or routine account verification without hinting at suspicion of money laundering.

clause_number: Chapter IV, Para 10 (Customer Acceptance Policy Controls)
text: Paragraph 10 of the RBI Master Direction on KYC (2016) establishes strict Customer Acceptance Policy rules. Regulated Entities must ensure that no account is opened in an anonymous or fictitious/benami name, no account is opened where the RE is unable to apply appropriate Customer Due Diligence measures due to customer non-cooperation or unreliability of documents, and transactions must not be permitted without identity verification where ML/TF risk is elevated. When an alert uncovers multiple intermediary accounts holding unverified identities, incomplete KYC files, or suspiciously aligned newly opened accounts, Para 10 principles bar clearing the network as routine benign activity. doc_title: RBI Master Direction — Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction, 2016 (updated 2024)
text: Paragraph 13 of the RBI Master Direction on KYC (2016) enumerates the mandatory triggers for undertaking Customer Due Diligence (CDD). Regulated Entities must execute CDD when establishing an account-based relationship, when carrying out an occasional transaction of an amount equal to or exceeding INR 50,000 (whether single or linked operations), when carrying out an international money transfer, when there is a suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing regardless of exemptions or thresholds, or when the RE has doubts about the veracity or adequacy of previously obtained customer identification data. Applying Enhanced Due Diligence requires verifying source of funds, source of wealth, beneficial ownership, and economic rationale whenever observed turnover diverges materially from declared annual income or occupation. Analysts record every verified KYC identifier, highlight unresolved income-to-volume discrepancies, and document enhanced ongoing monitoring recommendations.

doc_title: RBI Master Direction — Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction, 2016 (updated 2024)
clause_number: Chapter VI, Para 16 (Individual OVD & PAN Verification)
text: Paragraph 16 of the RBI Master Direction on KYC (2016) outlines Customer Due Diligence procedures for individuals, requiring verification of identity and address through Officially Valid Documents (OVDs)—such as Passport, Driving Licence, proof of possession of Aadhaar, Voter's Identity Card, NREGA job card, or National Population Register letter—together with Permanent Account Number (PAN) or Form 60. When an individual account lacks verified PAN or holds only simplified or minimal KYC documentation yet participates in high-value multi-hop electronic transfers, investigators must flag the KYC deficiency and recommend fresh CDD. Where an account participating in high-value inter-bank flows exhibits expired KYC records, minimal or small-account tiers, or missing PAN verification, analysts must surface the compliance gap in missing evidence and recommend requesting fresh OVD and PAN documentation rather than closing the alert as benign.

doc_title: RBI Master Direction — Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction, 2016 (updated 2024)
clause_number: Chapter VI, Para 16 & Part III (Legal Entity & Proprietorship CDD)
text: Under Chapter VI of the RBI Master Direction on KYC (2016), Customer Due Diligence for companies, partnership firms, trusts, and sole proprietorships requires independent verification of legal existence, registration status, authorized signatories, and beneficial ownership. For sole proprietorships, Regulated Entities must verify at least two business activity proofs such as GST registration certificate, municipal trade licence, or income tax return in the name of the firm. Confirming active MCA CIN, GSTIN, or statutory commercial registration is essential before accepting a commercial settlement narrative for scatter-gather fund flows. Corroborating a benign commercial hypothesis requires independent confirmation of active statutory registration (GSTIN, MCA CIN, or relevant sector licence) paired with recurring multi-month counterparty settlement history and alignment between observed payment ticket sizes and declared business turnover; a single registry flag alone is insufficient.

clause_number: Chapter VI, Para 18 (Video-Based Customer Identification Process — V-CIP)
text: Paragraph 18 of the RBI Master Direction on KYC (2016) governs the Video-based Customer Identification Process (V-CIP), an alternate consent-based method of establishing customer identity via seamless, secure, live audio-visual interaction with an official of the Regulated Entity. Accounts onboarded digitally via non-face-to-face channels without full V-CIP or in-person OVD verification carry elevated mule-account risk. If a newly opened digital savings account without full V-CIP suddenly executes rapid pass-through IMPS or RTGS transfers, investigators should apply Enhanced Due Diligence and treat mule-account typology as a primary suspicious hypothesis. Applying Enhanced Due Diligence requires verifying source of funds, source of wealth, beneficial ownership, and economic rationale whenever observed turnover diverges materially from declared annual income or occupation. Analysts record every verified KYC identifier, highlight unresolved income-to-volume discrepancies, and document enhanced ongoing monitoring recommendations.

doc_title: RBI Master Direction — Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction, 2016 (updated 2024)
clause_number: Chapter VI, Para 35 (EDD for Disproportionate Volume & Velocity)
text: Under the Enhanced Due Diligence and ongoing transaction monitoring provisions of the RBI Master Direction on KYC (Para 35 / Chapter VI), Regulated Entities must apply Enhanced Due Diligence whenever observed transaction volume, frequency, or velocity is disproportionate to the customer's declared annual income, stated occupation, business profile, and expected account turnover. A salaried individual or student declaring annual income of INR 4 to 6 lakhs whose account routes INR 15 to 50 lakhs across unrelated counterparties within days exhibits a material profile mismatch requiring source-of-funds verification and STR evaluation. Applying Enhanced Due Diligence requires verifying source of funds, source of wealth, beneficial ownership, and economic rationale whenever observed turnover diverges materially from declared annual income or occupation. Analysts record every verified KYC identifier, highlight unresolved income-to-volume discrepancies, and document enhanced ongoing monitoring recommendations.

doc_title: RBI Master Direction — Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction, 2016 (updated 2024)
clause_number: Chapter VI, Para 35 (Complex & Unusual Patterns Without Economic Rationale)
text: The RBI Master Direction on KYC directs Regulated Entities to pay special attention to all complex, unusually large transactions and all unusual patterns of transactions which have no apparent economic or visible lawful purpose. Banks must examine as far as possible the background and purpose of such transactions and record their findings in writing for at least five years. Multi-hop scatter-gather loops—where principal funds split across unrelated intermediaries and reconsolidate into one beneficiary—require documented scrutiny of both suspicious layering mechanics and plausible commercial settlement alternatives. Operational verification requires reconstructing candidate multi-hop paths across bounded lookback windows, checking exact decimal conservation between dispersed outflows and consolidated inflows, and testing whether intermediary accounts hold verified commercial registrations or recurring prior counterparty history before escalating an alert for Suspicious Transaction Report review.

doc_title: RBI Master Direction — Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction, 2016 (updated 2024)
clause_number: Chapter VI, Para 35 (Non-Face-to-Face & High-Risk Channel EDD)
text: Enhanced Due Diligence measures under Chapter VI, Part VI of the RBI Master Direction on KYC apply specifically to non-face-to-face customer onboarding (outside compliant V-CIP), accounts of Politically Exposed Persons, correspondent banking relationships, and clients operating cash-intensive or high-risk intermediary businesses. Additional EDD controls include verifying first payment through an existing KYC-compliant bank account, obtaining independent business registration checks, verifying source of wealth, and subjecting high-velocity outbound payment channels (IMPS/RTGS) to pre-clearance or post-transaction compliance review. Applying Enhanced Due Diligence requires verifying source of funds, source of wealth, beneficial ownership, and economic rationale whenever observed turnover diverges materially from declared annual income or occupation. Analysts record every verified KYC identifier, highlight unresolved income-to-volume discrepancies, and document enhanced ongoing monitoring recommendations.

text: When evaluating whether a high-value multi-counterparty fund flow represents legitimate commercial operations under the RBI Master Direction on KYC, analysts must corroborate documentary registration status (active GSTIN, MCA CIN, or Section 80G approval) alongside behavioral evidence such as historical counterparty relationships, recurring settlement cadence, and alignment between transaction amounts and declared business turnover. text: Enhanced Due Diligence under the RBI Master Direction on KYC requires verifying not merely the identity of the seed account holder, but also the economic relationship between the seed account and downstream counterparties. Inspecting multi-month counterparty transfer history helps distinguish recurring legitimate vendor, payroll, or marketplace settlements from one-off opportunistic mule pass-through bursts. Where a root account transacts exclusively with newly seen unrelated accounts over a compressed window and immediately depletes incoming credits, EDD findings weigh strongly toward STR escalation or formal information request. Applying Enhanced Due Diligence requires verifying source of funds, source of wealth, beneficial ownership, and economic rationale whenever observed turnover diverges materially from declared annual income or occupation. doc_title: RBI Master Direction — Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction, 2016 (updated 2024)
clause_number: Chapter V, Para 38 (Low, Medium, and High Risk Categorization)
text: Under the Risk Management provisions of the RBI Master Direction on KYC (Para 38 / Chapter V), Regulated Entities must categorize customers into Low, Medium, and High risk tiers based on assessment of customer identity, social and financial status, nature of business activity, location of the customer and counterparties, and expected transaction profile. Risk categorization must be dynamic rather than static: if an account originally onboarded as Low risk suddenly exhibits High-risk scatter-gather layering or rapid pass-through activity, the account's risk profile must be reassessed rather than relying blindly on its legacy Low-risk tag to dismiss the alert. Risk categorization guides monitoring intensity and periodic KYC refresh intervals (two years for High risk, eight years for Medium risk, ten years for Low risk) without serving as a standalone verdict. Investigators weigh risk tier alongside reconstructed fund-flow paths, commercial corroboration, and counterparty cadence when recommending disposition.

doc_title: RBI Master Direction — Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction, 2016 (updated 2024)
clause_number: Chapter V, Para 38 (Periodic Risk Review & High-Risk Triggers)
text: The RBI Master Direction on KYC mandates periodic review of customer risk categorization at least once every six months, with prompt upgrading to High risk whenever adverse transaction alerts, PEP associations, shell-entity indicators, or opaque ownership structures emerge. High-risk categorization triggers shorter KYC periodic updation cycles (every two years), stricter ongoing monitoring thresholds, and mandatory Enhanced Due Diligence before clearing unusual transfers. Importantly, high-risk status is an analytical risk factor—not standalone proof of suspicious activity—and must be weighed alongside actual fund-flow and commercial evidence. Risk categorization guides monitoring intensity and periodic KYC refresh intervals (two years for High risk, eight years for Medium risk, ten years for Low risk) without serving as a standalone verdict. Investigators weigh risk tier alongside reconstructed fund-flow paths, commercial corroboration, and counterparty cadence when recommending disposition.

doc_title: RBI Master Direction — Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction, 2016 (updated 2024)
clause_number: Chapter V, Para 38 (Avoiding Single-Attribute Disposition Shortcuts)
text: Risk-based supervision under the RBI Master Direction on KYC explicitly distinguishes risk categorization from transaction disposition. Categorizing a customer as High risk (for example, a bullion dealer, import-export firm, or cash-intensive business) mandates closer scrutiny and Enhanced Due Diligence, but does not automatically mean every transfer is suspicious. Conversely, a Low-risk salaried account compromised as a mule conduit can facilitate serious layering. Investigators must evaluate fund-flow topology, conservation math, counterparty cadence, and commercial corroboration together rather than deciding solely from KYC risk tier. Risk categorization guides monitoring intensity and periodic KYC refresh intervals (two years for High risk, eight years for Medium risk, ten years for Low risk) without serving as a standalone verdict. Investigators weigh risk tier alongside reconstructed fund-flow paths, commercial corroboration, and counterparty cadence when recommending disposition.

text: Paragraph 41 of the RBI Master Direction on KYC (2016), read with the Master Direction definitions, sets out mandatory Enhanced Due Diligence requirements for Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs)—individuals who are or have been entrusted with prominent public functions by a foreign country or domestic jurisdiction, including Heads of State or Government, senior politicians, senior government, judicial, or military officers, senior executives of state-owned corporations, and important political party officials. Regulated Entities must operate robust risk management systems to identify whether any customer or beneficial owner is a PEP or a close family member or associate of a PEP. Reviews involving Politically Exposed Persons or their close relatives and associates require verifying senior management approval on file, independently checking documented source of wealth against observed transfer volumes, and maintaining heightened continuous transaction monitoring over all linked domestic and cross-border accounts.

clause_number: Chapter VI, Para 41 (Senior Management Approval & Source of Wealth)
text: Under Paragraph 41 of the RBI Master Direction on KYC (2016), before establishing an account-based relationship with a Politically Exposed Person—or upon discovering that an existing customer or beneficial owner has subsequently become a PEP—Regulated Entities must obtain senior management approval to open or continue the business relationship. Regulated Entities must further take reasonable measures to establish the PEP's source of wealth and source of funds, and conduct continuous enhanced monitoring of the business relationship. Unexplained multi-hop transfers linked to a PEP account require escalated review and cannot be auto-closed. Reviews involving Politically Exposed Persons or their close relatives and associates require verifying senior management approval on file, independently checking documented source of wealth against observed transfer volumes, and maintaining heightened continuous transaction monitoring over all linked domestic and cross-border accounts.

text: Paragraph 41 of the RBI Master Direction on KYC (2016) extends PEP Enhanced Due Diligence safeguards to accounts of family members and close associates of Politically Exposed Persons. When scatter-gather intermediary or beneficiary accounts display family ties, shared addresses, or beneficial ownership links to a PEP alongside funds disproportionate to declared income, analysts must apply Para 41 EDD scrutiny and document source-of-wealth gaps. clause_number: Chapter VI, Para 46 (Periodic Updation Cycles: 2 / 8 / 10 Years)
text: Paragraph 46 of the RBI Master Direction on KYC (2016) prescribes risk-based periodic updation of KYC records at least once every two years for High-risk customers, once every eight years for Medium-risk customers, and once every ten years for Low-risk customers from the date of account opening or last KYC updation. For legal entities, periodic updation includes confirming no change in beneficial ownership, registration status, or principal business activity. Accounts overdue for periodic KYC updation that suddenly exhibit high-value inter-bank scatter-gather activity require fresh Customer Due Diligence before benign closure.
